prompt.context: Your client is Deda Mitsa Winery, a mid-size wine producer in the Republic of Georgia. They produce ten million bottles of wine annually and are moderately profitable. They enjoy a reputation as a high quality wine producer; many of Deda Mitsa Winery's competitors are known to import grapes and pass them off as Georgian in their wines. Even though Georgian wine is largely unknown in many parts of the world, it is one of the most prized wines of the former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. However, Russia has recently declared a moratorium on imports of Georgian wine due to the prevalence of counterfeits. Deda Mitsa Winery usually exports 50% of its wines to Russia and is uncertain where to make up the difference.
prompt.question: What options are available to the company?

clarifying_info.q: Where does the rest of the wine go (besides Russia)?
clarifying_info.a: 30% is sold to Ukraine and 20% is sold domestically.

clarifying_info.q: What is Deda Mitsa Winery's market share?
clarifying_info.a: Overall, 100 million bottles of Georgian wine are produced every year, giving Deda Mitsa Winery a 10% market share.

clarifying_info.q: How strong is the domestic market?
clarifying_info.a: The potential of the domestic market is limited because many Georgians make wine at home.

clarifying_info.q: What is the wine consumption level in potential target countries?

framework: Assess options to offset lost Russia volume: raise prices, shut down, pivot to alternate grape products, seek embargo exemption, expand domestically, or export to new markets
Steer toward export to new markets as primary lever
Identify and shortlist target export markets using consumption volume and growth data
Evaluate profitability of each candidate market (COGS + shipping + tariffs + marketing vs. achievable price)
Assess willingness-to-pay by benchmarking breakeven price against competitor prices in each market
Make a market recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Brainstorm all options available to Deda Mitsa Winery to replace the lost Russia volume.
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: raise prices on remaining sales, shut down/scale back, move into alternate grape products not covered by the embargo (juice, vodka), seek an embargo exemption based on quality reputation, export to new markets, expand domestic sales. Candidate should then be steered toward exploring new export markets.

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, which 2–3 countries are the strongest candidates for Deda Mitsa Winery's export strategy? What additional factors should they consider?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read both current consumption and growth rate together. Georgian wine has little fame outside the former Soviet Union, so competing in France is unattractive. USA has high growth but strong international competition. Estonia and Romania emerge as strongest candidates: they are former Soviet-sphere markets where Georgian wine has a reputation advantage, and consumption data is favorable. Additional factors: cost of shipping, wine preferences (dry/sweet), GDP, risk of additional embargos, reputation of Georgian wine in that country, political and economic stability, distribution networks, corruption level.

questions.prompt: How much will Deda Mitsa Winery have to charge per bottle in each of Estonia, Romania, and USA in order to break even, assuming all Russia-bound bottles are redirected to one new market?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate total volume lost from Russia (5MM bottles), apply COGS per bottle, then add country-specific marketing, tariff, and shipping costs. Divide total cost by 5MM bottles to get breakeven price per bottle for each country.

math.setup: Russia volume = 10MM bottles x 50% = 5MM bottles. COGS = wine 5 lari + bottle 0.5 lari + label 0.1 lari = 5.6 lari/bottle. Total COGS = 5MM x 5.6 = 28MM lari. Add country costs: Estonia (marketing 1MM, tariffs 1MM, shipping 5 lari/bottle); Romania (marketing 7MM, tariffs 20MM, shipping 5 lari/bottle); USA (marketing 12MM, tariffs 0MM, shipping 10 lari/bottle).
math.answer: Estonia: 11 lari/bottle; Romania: 16 lari/bottle; USA: 18 lari/bottle

questions.prompt: What information do you need in order to determine whether these prices are reasonable?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for competitor prices or average market prices in each target country. Present Exhibit 3. Candidate should note: Romania's breakeven (16 lari) is higher than what most Romanians regularly pay; Estonia's breakeven (11 lari) is within what most Estonians will pay; USA's breakeven (18 lari) is higher than the other two but still within range of what Americans will pay for wine.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should Deda Mitsa Winery consider when deciding which new market to export to?

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Reputation of Georgian wine in that country
Strength of incumbent local and international wine brands

categories.name: Cost and logistics
ideas: Marketing spend required to establish brand

categories.name: Risk factors
ideas: Risk of additional embargos or trade restrictions

recommendation: Export to Estonia first: lowest breakeven price (11 lari/bottle), favorable willingness-to-pay, former Soviet-sphere market where Georgian wine has existing recognition, and positive consumption growth.
USA is a viable second option given strong growth and willingness to pay up to 18 lari, though it requires higher marketing investment and more brand-building effort.
Romania is the weakest near-term option: breakeven price (16 lari) exceeds what most Romanians typically pay for wine.
risks: Estonian market is relatively small — may not fully absorb all 5MM bottles; may need to split volume across markets
Additional diplomatic or trade risks could extend or expand the embargo beyond Russia
Brand building in new markets takes time; short-term revenue shortfall is likely
Competition from established Western European and local wines in all target markets
next_steps: Conduct detailed market sizing for Estonia (population x willingness-to-pay) to confirm it can absorb the 5MM bottle volume
Map existing distribution networks and identify potential partners in Estonia and the USA
Develop a marketing and branding plan emphasizing authenticity and quality differentiation
Monitor Russian embargo situation for potential reversal or negotiated exemption based on quality reputation
Explore whether volume can be split across Estonia and USA to reduce single-market concentration risk
